business_question: You are supporting a New York Times editor who is fact-checking a reporter's proposed statement that the Titanic evacuation followed a 'women and children first' practice. Using the supplied Titanic passenger dataset, determine what the data show about the relationship between sex and survival. Give a numerical answer using survivor counts, survival rates, the percentage-point difference, and the relative survival rate. Create one chart illustrating the result for the editor. Distinguish an observed association from proof that a particular evacuation policy or order caused the result, and identify briefly what this dataset alone cannot establish.
business_answer_shown: In the supplied 1,309-passenger dataset, 339 of 466 female passengers survived (72.7%) and 161 of 843 male passengers survived (19.1%). Female survival was 53.6 percentage points higher; female / male survival rate = 3.81×, calculated from unrounded rates. This is an observed sex-survival association across all ages. Children's outcomes are untested in this comparison, and the association alone cannot establish evacuation policy, boarding order, or cause.

data_fidelity_checks.check: Required input integrity and business-question preservation
data_fidelity_checks.notes: Read all five RUN NOTE inputs. The question contains the full instructor request, not a placeholder, and is reproduced verbatim apart from trailing whitespace. The principles PDF governs; case-study instructions and policy framing were treated as illustrative material.

Titanic.xlsx, Sheet1: 1,309 data rows. Recorded sex has female (466) and male (843); survived has 1 (survived, 500) and 0 (did not survive, 809). Both fields have zero missing or unexpected values. All ages are included; zero rows were excluded or recoded.

Age contains 263 NA entries; embarked contains 2 NA entries; home.dest contains 564 empty cells. These fields are not used in the sex-survival calculation. All affected records remain included; no child threshold or age-group analysis was introduced.
Recomputed from spreadsheet rows: female = 339 / 466 = 72.746781%; male = 161 / 843 = 19.098458%. Survivor counts sum to 500 and group denominators sum to 1,309.

Female minus male = 53.648323 percentage points, displayed as 53.6 percentage points. Female / male survival rate = (339/466)/(161/843) = 3.809040, displayed as 3.81×. Neither comparison was calculated from rounded labels.

Bar heights use unrounded spreadsheet rates on a shared 0–100% axis. Direct labels show 72.7%, 19.1%, and each survivor/group total. The title and ratio are verified; notes define all-age groups, name Titanic.xlsx and n, disclose no exclusions and 263 missing ages, and specify one-decimal rates/gap and a two-decimal ratio.

The title states an observational difference. The subtitle defines the metric and all-age sex groups. Visible notes identify children's outcomes as untested and state that this association cannot establish evacuation policy, boarding order, or cause. No significance, historical mechanism, or policy conclusion is asserted.

Observed survival outcomes alone cannot establish evacuation policy, boarding order, implementation of a practice, or cause. No significance testing or adjustment for other passenger characteristics was performed.
The result describes the supplied 1,309 passenger records. The spreadsheet supplies no documentation establishing coverage of other populations, including crew.

The principles workbook emphasizes presentation props, and the case study illustrates policy advocacy. This case requires a readable standalone editorial chart; essential evidence and limits take precedence over omitting notes or adopting advocacy framing.
